## 1.0 Network Fundamentals

### Objective 1.1 — Network component roles

<a id="question-1-1-a"></a>

#### 1.1-a

[Study objective 1.1](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-1)

Which device normally forwards a frame inside one VLAN using a MAC address table?

- **A.** Layer 2 switch
- **B.** DNS server
- **C.** Wireless client
- **D.** Router routing process

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Layer 2 switch**

A Layer 2 switch keeps a local directory of MAC addresses and ports. It learns where senders are heard, then uses the receiver's destination MAC to choose the outgoing port within that VLAN.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-1-poe-budget"></a>

#### expanded-1.1-poe-budget

[Study objective 1.1](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-1)

A switch has eight powered ports, but the ninth compatible AP receives no power. The AP works on an unused port of another switch. Which check best follows this evidence?

- **A.** Check the first switch's remaining PoE power budget and port power status.
- **B.** Replace the wireless controller because it supplies Ethernet power.
- **C.** Assign the AP a public IPv4 address.
- **D.** Change the AP's DNS domain before inspecting power.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Check the first switch's remaining PoE power budget and port power status.**

The AP receives power elsewhere, so start with the original port and the switch's remaining power allowance. PoE requires both a compatible port and enough available watts. IP settings cannot turn on an AP that has no power.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-1-inline-ips"></a>

#### expanded-1.1-inline-ips

[Study objective 1.1](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-1)

A company wants malicious traffic blocked before it reaches a server. Which component directly inspects and can stop that traffic while deployed in the forwarding path?

- **A.** A passive packet-capture station with no enforcement link.
- **B.** A DNS server that only answers name queries.
- **C.** A patch panel joining two copper cables.
- **D.** An inline intrusion prevention system.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. An inline intrusion prevention system.**

Inline means the traffic actually passes through the device. An intrusion prevention system there can inspect and stop matching attacks before delivery. A passive observer can report what it saw but cannot itself drop traffic on that path.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-1-server-versus-network"></a>

#### expanded-1.1-server-versus-network

[Study objective 1.1](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-1)

A client can ping a server, but its HTTPS connection is refused. Which conclusion is supported?

- **A.** Successful ping proves every server application is working.
- **B.** An access point must perform the server's TLS handshake.
- **C.** IP reachability exists, but the HTTPS service or its access policy still needs investigation.
- **D.** The server must be physically disconnected.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. IP reachability exists, but the HTTPS service or its access policy still needs investigation.**

Ping and HTTPS test different functions. A successful ping shows IP request/reply reachability for that test; a refused HTTPS connection can still mean the web service is stopped, not listening or rejected by policy.

</details>

### Objective 1.2 — Network topology architectures

<a id="question-1-2-a"></a>

#### 1.2-a

[Study objective 1.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-2)

Which architecture connects every leaf switch to every spine switch?

- **A.** Three-tier campus
- **B.** Spine–leaf
- **C.** Daisy chain
- **D.** SOHO

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Spine–leaf**

In spine–leaf, every leaf has a connection to every spine. A server on one leaf can normally reach a server on another through one spine, giving a predictable path pattern.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-2-collapsed-core-roles"></a>

#### expanded-1.2-collapsed-core-roles

[Study objective 1.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-2)

A small campus combines distribution and core functions in one resilient switch pair. What topology does this describe?

- **A.** A single shared coaxial collision domain.
- **B.** A two-tier campus with a collapsed core.
- **C.** A three-tier campus with three separate switching layers.
- **D.** A leaf-spine fabric with no distribution functions.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. A two-tier campus with a collapsed core.**

The access layer connects users. Combining distribution and core functions leaves one other functional tier, called a collapsed core. Counting physical boxes or floors does not tell you the number of architectural tiers.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-2-cloud-responsibility"></a>

#### expanded-1.2-cloud-responsibility

[Study objective 1.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-2)

A team rents virtual machines and installs and patches the guest operating systems itself. Which cloud service model most closely fits?

- **A.** Infrastructure as a Service.
- **B.** Software as a Service with no guest OS management.
- **C.** A physical-only campus with no virtual resources.
- **D.** A DNS record type that creates virtual machines.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Infrastructure as a Service.**

In IaaS, the provider supplies infrastructure while the customer normally operates the guest OS and applications. SaaS instead supplies a finished application, and PaaS manages more of the application platform for the customer.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-2-three-tier-core"></a>

#### expanded-1.2-three-tier-core

[Study objective 1.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-2)

In a three-tier campus, access switches connect users and distribution switches apply policy. What is the core layer's main design role?

- **A.** Assign every endpoint its wireless passphrase.
- **B.** Replace the access layer's endpoint connections.
- **C.** Store all dynamically learned DNS records.
- **D.** Provide resilient, fast connectivity between distribution blocks.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Provide resilient, fast connectivity between distribution blocks.**

The core is the reliable, fast connection between distribution areas. User attachments belong at access and aggregation/policy at distribution; separating those jobs helps the larger design scale.

</details>

### Objective 1.3 — Physical interfaces and cabling

<a id="question-1-3-a"></a>

#### 1.3-a

[Study objective 1.3](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-3)

Which medium is generally preferred for a long-distance optical link?

- **A.** Unshielded twisted pair
- **B.** Single-mode fiber
- **C.** Console rollover cable
- **D.** Coaxial bus

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Single-mode fiber**

Single-mode fiber is designed for longer optical distances with compatible long-reach transceivers. The cable and both end devices must support the same optical standard; the connector fitting is not enough.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-3-optical-compatibility"></a>

#### expanded-1.3-optical-compatibility

[Study objective 1.3](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-3)

Both ends of a fiber link use supported transceivers, but one end is 10G single-mode at 1310 nm and the other is 10G multimode at 850 nm. What must be corrected?

- **A.** Enable TCP acknowledgments on the transceivers.
- **B.** Use a larger IPv4 subnet to increase optical compatibility.
- **C.** Match the optical standards and use their supported fiber type.
- **D.** Set both switch ports to the same native VLAN to match wavelengths.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. Match the optical standards and use their supported fiber type.**

Both ends say 10G, but they use different light wavelengths and fiber standards. Match the supported optical signaling at both ends and install the appropriate fiber; nominal speed and a fitting connector are insufficient.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-3-copper-interference"></a>

#### expanded-1.3-copper-interference

[Study objective 1.3](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-3)

A new access cable must cross an electrically noisy industrial area. Which medium inherently avoids electromagnetic interference in its signal path?

- **A.** Any copper cable after disabling CDP.
- **B.** Optical fiber.
- **C.** Unshielded copper twisted pair because it carries no electrical signal.
- **D.** A copper console rollover cable used as an Ethernet uplink.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Optical fiber.**

Fiber carries light, so electrical noise does not interfere with its data signal as it can with copper's electrical signal. The design still needs suitable distance, optics and installation practices.

</details>

### Objective 1.4 — Interface and cable faults

<a id="question-1-4-a"></a>

#### 1.4-a

[Study objective 1.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-4)

A port shows many CRC errors. What should you investigate first?

- **A.** DNS recursion
- **B.** Cable or physical-link integrity
- **C.** OSPF router ID
- **D.** DHCP lease time

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Cable or physical-link integrity**

A CRC error means a received Ethernet frame failed its corruption check. Start with cable/optical integrity and compatible link settings at both ends, then see whether new errors still appear.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-4-duplex-mismatch"></a>

#### expanded-1.4-duplex-mismatch

[Study objective 1.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-4)

One end of a legacy Ethernet link is forced to full duplex; the other operates at half duplex. The link is up but performs poorly under load. What is the best repair?

- **A.** Use matching duplex settings, normally compatible autonegotiation at both ends.
- **B.** Keep the mismatch and increase the OSPF process ID.
- **C.** Add an unrelated DNS server to remove collisions.
- **D.** Force a different native VLAN on each end.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Use matching duplex settings, normally compatible autonegotiation at both ends.**

Half duplex takes turns; full duplex permits simultaneous sending and receiving. Mismatched ends can show an up link yet perform badly. Restore compatible settings, normally supported autonegotiation at both ends, then recheck new error counters.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-4-administrative-shutdown"></a>

#### expanded-1.4-administrative-shutdown

[Study objective 1.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-4)

IOS XE reports an Ethernet interface as administratively down, line protocol down. Which fact should be checked before replacing the cable?

- **A.** Whether an OSPF DR has a higher router ID.
- **B.** Whether the DNS zone contains a CNAME.
- **C.** Whether a trunk uses the reserved VLAN 4095.
- **D.** Whether the interface is intentionally shut down in configuration.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Whether the interface is intentionally shut down in configuration.**

Administratively down means configuration has disabled the port. First confirm whether shutdown was intended. Use no shutdown only when the design calls for enabling it; replacing the cable does not remove the configured shutdown.

</details>

### Objective 1.5 — TCP and UDP

<a id="question-1-5-a"></a>

#### 1.5-a

[Study objective 1.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-5)

Which function is supplied by TCP but not by UDP itself?

- **A.** IP addressing
- **B.** Reliable ordered byte-stream delivery
- **C.** MAC learning
- **D.** Route selection

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Reliable ordered byte-stream delivery**

TCP numbers the bytes it sends, checks acknowledgments and resends missing data. These mechanisms provide ordered, reliable delivery. UDP itself does not provide them, although an application can add similar checks.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-3"></a>

#### extra-3

[Study objective 1.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-5)

Which flags establish a TCP connection?

- **A.** SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
- **B.** FIN, FIN, RST
- **C.** ACK, RST, FIN
- **D.** UDP, IP, TCP

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK**

The TCP client starts with SYN. The server answers SYN-ACK, acknowledging that start and supplying its own synchronization. The client completes setup with ACK. This is the three-way handshake.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-5-dhcp-udp"></a>

#### expanded-1.5-dhcp-udp

[Study objective 1.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-5)

A packet capture shows a DHCPv4 client discovery exchange. Which transport and port direction should be expected for the initial client message?

- **A.** UDP from server port 67 toward client port 68 for the client's first message.
- **B.** TCP port 443 because DHCP always runs over HTTPS.
- **C.** UDP from client port 68 toward server port 67.
- **D.** TCP from client port 68 toward server port 67.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. UDP from client port 68 toward server port 67.**

The initial DHCPv4 client message uses UDP source port 68 and destination port 67. A client without its assigned address can use a broadcast; it does not establish a TCP connection for this exchange.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-5-udp-application-reliability"></a>

#### expanded-1.5-udp-application-reliability

[Study objective 1.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-5)

A developer uses UDP for a transaction that still needs lost responses detected. Which design statement is correct?

- **A.** The use of UDP prevents all reliability logic at higher layers.
- **B.** The application can implement acknowledgments, timeouts and retries above UDP.
- **C.** UDP will automatically retransmit every missing application response.
- **D.** UDP guarantees application messages arrive in order.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. The application can implement acknowledgments, timeouts and retries above UDP.**

UDP does not track reliable ordered delivery itself. The application can add confirmation messages, wait timers and retries to detect missing responses, choosing the extra overhead and timing behavior it needs.

</details>

### Objective 1.6 — IPv4 addresses and subnetting

<a id="question-1-6-a"></a>

#### 1.6-a

[Study objective 1.6](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-6)

What is the network address of 192.168.10.77/26?

- **A.** 192.168.10.0
- **B.** 192.168.10.64
- **C.** 192.168.10.76
- **D.** 192.168.10.128

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. 192.168.10.64**

1. A /26 leaves 32 − 26 = 6 host bits. 2. That gives 2^6 = 64 addresses per block. 3. The last-number blocks are 0–63, 64–127, 128–191 and 192–255. 77 belongs to 64–127, so the network is 192.168.10.64.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-0"></a>

#### extra-0

[Study objective 1.6](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-6)

How many traditionally usable host addresses does a /27 provide?

- **A.** 14
- **B.** 30
- **C.** 62
- **D.** 126

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. 30**

A /27 leaves 32 − 27 = 5 host bits. 2^5 gives 32 total addresses. On an ordinary IPv4 subnet, subtract the network and broadcast addresses: 32 − 2 = 30 usable host addresses.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-1"></a>

#### extra-1

[Study objective 1.6](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-6)

What is the broadcast address of 10.0.0.130/25?

- **A.** 10.0.0.127
- **B.** 10.0.0.128
- **C.** 10.0.0.254
- **D.** 10.0.0.255

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. 10.0.0.255**

A /25 has 128 addresses per block. Last-number ranges are 0–127 and 128–255. 130 belongs to the second block, whose final address is 10.0.0.255; that final address is its broadcast.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-2"></a>

#### extra-2

[Study objective 1.6](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-6)

Which mask corresponds to /28?

- **A.** 255.255.255.240
- **B.** 255.255.255.224
- **C.** 255.255.255.192
- **D.** 255.255.255.248

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. 255.255.255.240**

/28 uses 24 network bits in the first three numbers and four in the last. Those last four positions have weights 128, 64, 32 and 16. Their sum is 240, so the mask is 255.255.255.240.

</details>

<a id="question-alignment-1"></a>

#### alignment-1

[Study objective 1.6](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-6)

A /16 must supply equal subnets for at least 500 ordinary usable hosts each. What is the longest suitable prefix?

- **A.** /24
- **B.** /23
- **C.** /25
- **D.** /26

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. /23**

Nine host bits give 2^9 − 2 = 510 ordinary usable addresses, enough for 500. That leaves a /23 prefix. A /24 leaves only eight host bits and 254 usable addresses, which is too small. Inside the original /16, seven bits remain to identify 128 equal /23 subnets.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-6-gateway-same-subnet"></a>

#### expanded-1.6-gateway-same-subnet

[Study objective 1.6](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-6)

A host is configured as 192.0.2.70/27. Which proposed default gateway is in the same subnet and is an ordinary usable host address?

- **A.** 192.0.2.65.
- **B.** 192.0.2.63.
- **C.** 192.0.2.95.
- **D.** 192.0.2.97.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. 192.0.2.65.**

A /27 has 32-address blocks. .70 falls in .64–.95; .64 names the network and .95 is broadcast. Ordinary hosts, including this host's gateway, use .65–.94. Thus .65 fits, while .63 and .97 are outside the block.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-6-vlsm-nonoverlap"></a>

#### expanded-1.6-vlsm-nonoverlap

[Study objective 1.6](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-6)

A VLSM plan already uses 10.20.0.0/25 and 10.20.0.128/26. Which /27 can be added without overlapping either allocation?

- **A.** 10.20.0.64/27.
- **B.** 10.20.0.128/27.
- **C.** 10.20.0.160/27.
- **D.** 10.20.0.192/27.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. 10.20.0.192/27.**

The existing /25 uses .0–.127 and the existing /26 uses .128–.191. The next free /27 block is .192–.223. A smaller subnet inside either used range would still allocate some of the same addresses twice.

</details>

### Objective 1.7 — Private IPv4 address space

<a id="question-1-7-a"></a>

#### 1.7-a

[Study objective 1.7](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-7)

Which address is in an RFC 1918 private range?

- **A.** 172.32.1.1
- **B.** 172.20.1.1
- **C.** 169.254.10.1
- **D.** 11.0.0.1

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. 172.20.1.1**

The private block 172.16.0.0/12 includes second-number values 16 through 31. Because 20 is in that interval, 172.20.1.1 belongs to the private range. Not every address beginning with 172 is private.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-7-private-address-security"></a>

#### expanded-1.7-private-address-security

[Study objective 1.7](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-7)

A server uses an RFC 1918 address behind a translating gateway. What security conclusion follows from that addressing choice alone?

- **A.** The server no longer needs operating-system updates.
- **B.** Every Internet router will advertise the server's private subnet.
- **C.** None of the application access policy is proven; filtering and authentication must still be designed.
- **D.** All inbound and outbound attacks are automatically prevented.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. None of the application access policy is proven; filtering and authentication must still be designed.**

Private addressing controls address allocation and normal public routing, not the complete access policy. It does not encrypt traffic or authenticate users. Decide and verify firewall, login and host protections separately.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-7-private-site-overlap"></a>

#### expanded-1.7-private-site-overlap

[Study objective 1.7](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-7)

Two companies both use 10.40.0.0/16 and now want direct routed connectivity between their networks. What issue must the integration plan address?

- **A.** OSPF always combines overlapping companies into a unique public subnet.
- **B.** Overlapping address space makes destinations ambiguous and needs a deliberate design solution.
- **C.** RFC 1918 guarantees private prefixes are globally unique.
- **D.** Changing DNS TTLs automatically makes overlapping routes distinct.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Overlapping address space makes destinations ambiguous and needs a deliberate design solution.**

Both sites have the same destination block, so ordinary routing cannot tell which identically addressed host is intended. Plan unique addressing or a deliberate translation/isolation solution before joining the networks.

</details>

### Objective 1.8 — IPv6 addresses and prefixes

<a id="question-1-8-a"></a>

#### 1.8-a

[Study objective 1.8](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-8)

Which is a valid compression of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?

- **A.** 2001:db8::1
- **B.** 2001::db8::1
- **C.** 2001:db8:1
- **D.** 2001:db8:::1

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. 2001:db8::1**

Remove unnecessary zeros at the start of each four-digit group: 0db8 becomes db8 and 0001 becomes 1. Replace the consecutive all-zero groups with one ::. The result is 2001:db8::1; only one :: is allowed per address.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-8-ipv6-default-router-ra"></a>

#### expanded-1.8-ipv6-default-router-ra

[Study objective 1.8](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-8)

An IPv6 host learns an address through SLAAC. Which information normally identifies its default router?

- **A.** The source link-local address of a suitable Router Advertisement.
- **B.** A DHCPv6 option that is required to carry every IPv6 default gateway.
- **C.** An IPv4 ARP reply containing an IPv6 broadcast address.
- **D.** The first public DNS server returned by a query.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. The source link-local address of a suitable Router Advertisement.**

A suitable Router Advertisement tells the host about a potential default router using the router's link-local source address. DHCPv6 can supply an address or other settings, but it does not replace this default-router discovery role.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-8-ios-ipv6-routing"></a>

#### expanded-1.8-ios-ipv6-routing

[Study objective 1.8](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-8)

Two IOS XE router interfaces have valid IPv6 addresses and are up, but IPv6 unicast forwarding between them has not been enabled globally. Which command enables that routing function?

- **A.** ip routing ipv6-only
- **B.** ipv6 enable all-switchports
- **C.** router ospf ipv6-default-gateway
- **D.** ipv6 unicast-routing

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. ipv6 unicast-routing**

ipv6 unicast-routing is the global switch enabling IPv6 packet forwarding between networks. Assigning interface addresses and bringing links up are separate steps and do not automatically enable that global routing function.

</details>

### Objective 1.9 — IPv6 address categories

<a id="question-1-9-a"></a>

#### 1.9-a

[Study objective 1.9](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-9)

Which prefix identifies IPv6 link-local unicast addresses?

- **A.** ff00::/8
- **B.** fe80::/10
- **C.** 2000::/3
- **D.** fc00::/7

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. fe80::/10**

fe80::/10 marks IPv6 link-local addresses. They work only on their local link, so routers do not forward them to another link. A device with several interfaces may also need the outgoing interface named.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-4"></a>

#### extra-4

[Study objective 1.9](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-9)

Which IPv6 address reaches all routers on the local link?

- **A.** ff02::1
- **B.** ff02::2
- **C.** ::1
- **D.** fe80::1

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. ff02::2**

ff02::2 is the IPv6 all-routers multicast group on the local link. ff02::1 is all IPv6 nodes on that link. The group address identifies the intended set of receivers.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-9-modified-eui64"></a>

#### expanded-1.9-modified-eui64

[Study objective 1.9](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-9)

Using modified EUI-64, what interface identifier is derived from MAC address 00:11:22:33:44:55?

- **A.** 0011:22ff:fe33:4455.
- **B.** 0211:2233:fffe:4455.
- **C.** 0211:22ff:fe33:4455.
- **D.** 0011:2233:4455:0000.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. 0211:22ff:fe33:4455.**

1. Split 00:11:22:33:44:55 in half. 2. Insert ff:fe: 00:11:22:ff:fe:33:44:55. 3. Flip the specified universal/local bit so the first byte changes from 00 to 02. 4. Group pairs of bytes into IPv6 groups: 0211:22ff:fe33:4455. Other interface-ID methods are also common.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-9-anycast-delivery"></a>

#### expanded-1.9-anycast-delivery

[Study objective 1.9](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-9)

Several IPv6 service nodes deliberately share the same anycast address. How is a packet to that address normally delivered?

- **A.** Only to the node whose MAC address supplied the address.
- **B.** To one instance selected by the routing topology.
- **C.** To every instance through an IPv6 broadcast.
- **D.** To every instance through mandatory multicast replication.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. To one instance selected by the routing topology.**

Anycast gives several service instances the same unicast-format address. Routing chooses one reachable instance for a packet. It does not copy that packet to every instance as group delivery would.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-9-unique-local-scope"></a>

#### expanded-1.9-unique-local-scope

[Study objective 1.9](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-9)

A site uses fd42:10:20::/48 for internal IPv6 subnets. Which description fits this prefix?

- **A.** Unique local addressing intended for local use, without an expectation of global Internet routing.
- **B.** Link-local addressing that routers must never forward between local subnets.
- **C.** A multicast range for all routers on a link.
- **D.** An IPv4-mapped address that requires NAT44.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Unique local addressing intended for local use, without an expectation of global Internet routing.**

fd00::/8 is the commonly locally assigned part of fc00::/7 unique-local addressing. These addresses can route between internal subnets; they are not intended for global public routing. Link-local is different because it stays on one link.

</details>

### Objective 1.10 — Client operating-system IP settings

<a id="question-1-10-a"></a>

#### 1.10-a

[Study objective 1.10](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-10)

A client reaches 1.1.1.1 but cannot resolve example.com. What should be checked next?

- **A.** DNS configuration
- **B.** Switch root priority
- **C.** EtherChannel mode
- **D.** Fiber wavelength

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. DNS configuration**

Reaching a remote IP address shows that an IP path works for that test. Looking up a name is DNS's separate job, so check the configured DNS servers, their reachability and their answers next.

</details>

<a id="question-alignment-3"></a>

#### alignment-3

[Study objective 1.10](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-10)

A server answers WAN-sourced ping but not LAN-sourced ping from the same router. What should be checked?

- **A.** Only DNS
- **B.** The remote return route and policy for the LAN prefix
- **C.** Whether all switches share a MAC
- **D.** Whether OSPF process IDs equal port numbers

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. The remote return route and policy for the LAN prefix**

A reply is addressed back to the source used in the test. The server may know a route and permit traffic back to the WAN address while lacking that route or permission for the LAN subnet.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-10-linux-route-check"></a>

#### expanded-1.10-linux-route-check

[Study objective 1.10](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-10)

A Linux host reaches local neighbors but cannot reach any remote subnet. Which command directly displays its default-route selection?

- **A.** show vlan brief
- **B.** dig -x localhost
- **C.** spanning-tree root primary
- **D.** ip route show default

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. ip route show default**

ip route show default displays the Linux host's default route. Reaching neighbors on the same subnet does not prove a default gateway exists or works, because those local deliveries do not need it.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-10-macos-interface-check"></a>

#### expanded-1.10-macos-interface-check

[Study objective 1.10](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-10)

On macOS, an administrator needs to verify an interface's configured IP address and netmask. Which command is appropriate?

- **A.** Get-NetIPAddress
- **B.** switchport access vlan 20
- **C.** ifconfig en0
- **D.** show ip interface brief

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. ifconfig en0**

ifconfig en0 displays that macOS interface's address, mask and status. Check the actual interface name on the machine; commands for IOS or Windows are not native substitutes for this macOS inspection.

</details>

### Objective 1.11 — Wireless networking principles

<a id="question-1-11-a"></a>

#### 1.11-a

[Study objective 1.11](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-11)

Which 2.4 GHz channel set is commonly nonoverlapping with 20 MHz channels?

- **A.** 1, 2, 3
- **B.** 1, 6, 11
- **C.** 3, 6, 9
- **D.** 8, 9, 10

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. 1, 6, 11**

For common 20 MHz 2.4 GHz networks, channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap one another in many regions. This helps neighboring access points reuse radio spectrum; legal channels and the local environment still matter.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-11-ssid-versus-encryption"></a>

#### expanded-1.11-ssid-versus-encryption

[Study objective 1.11](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-11)

Two APs advertise the same SSID. What does matching the SSID alone prove about their encryption settings?

- **A.** Clients are guaranteed seamless authenticated roaming.
- **B.** Nothing; security settings must be checked independently.
- **C.** Both APs necessarily use WPA3-Personal.
- **D.** Both APs necessarily share a radio channel.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Nothing; security settings must be checked independently.**

An SSID is only the wireless network name. Two access points can advertise the same name while using different login methods, encryption or VLAN policies. Inspect those settings independently.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-11-channel-width-reuse"></a>

#### expanded-1.11-channel-width-reuse

[Study objective 1.11](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-11)

An administrator increases channel width while keeping the available RF spectrum unchanged. What design trade-off should be considered?

- **A.** Wider channels can improve potential link throughput but leave fewer independent channels for reuse.
- **B.** Wider channels always create more nonoverlapping channels.
- **C.** Channel width removes the need to plan neighboring AP channels.
- **D.** Channel width changes the IPv4 subnet mask of each client.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Wider channels can improve potential link throughput but leave fewer independent channels for reuse.**

A wider channel occupies more of the available radio spectrum. It may carry more on one good link, but leaves fewer independent channels for nearby access points and can increase competition in a dense network.

</details>

### Objective 1.12 — Virtual machines, containers and VRFs

<a id="question-1-12-a"></a>

#### 1.12-a

[Study objective 1.12](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-12)

What does a VRF isolate?

- **A.** Ethernet voltage
- **B.** IP routing tables
- **C.** DNS record types
- **D.** TCP sequence numbers

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. IP routing tables**

A VRF is a separate IP route list inside one routing device. Interfaces in different VRFs do not automatically route between one another just because they share the same hardware.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-12-container-versus-vm"></a>

#### expanded-1.12-container-versus-vm

[Study objective 1.12](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-12)

A server runs several containers and several full virtual machines. Which distinction is normally correct?

- **A.** Every container requires a separate physical CPU.
- **B.** Full VMs must all share the same guest kernel.
- **C.** Containers provide physical separation equivalent to separate buildings.
- **D.** Containers share the host kernel; full VMs can each run their own guest kernel.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Containers share the host kernel; full VMs can each run their own guest kernel.**

A full VM can run its own guest operating-system kernel, the core part of that OS. Containers share the host kernel while isolating application processes. Those designs have different resource costs and isolation boundaries.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-12-hypervisor-role"></a>

#### expanded-1.12-hypervisor-role

[Study objective 1.12](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-12)

A physical server hosts three virtual machines, each seeing virtual CPUs and memory. Which component allocates those physical resources to the guests?

- **A.** The DNS recursive resolver.
- **B.** The campus spanning-tree root port.
- **C.** The hypervisor.
- **D.** The Ethernet MAC aging timer.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. The hypervisor.**

The hypervisor presents virtual hardware and divides real processor, memory and input/output resources among the VMs. A virtual switch handles guest networking instead; it does not allocate the guest processors or memory.

</details>

### Objective 1.13 — Ethernet switching behavior

<a id="question-1-13-a"></a>

#### 1.13-a

[Study objective 1.13](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-13)

Which field does a switch use to learn its dynamic MAC table?

- **A.** Destination IP
- **B.** Source MAC
- **C.** Destination TCP port
- **D.** Source IP

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Source MAC**

When a frame arrives, the switch reads its source MAC and remembers the arrival port and VLAN. That is learning. It later uses the destination MAC to decide where to deliver a frame.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-5"></a>

#### extra-5

[Study objective 1.13](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-13)

What does a switch do with unknown unicast traffic?

- **A.** Drops it always
- **B.** Floods eligible ports in the same VLAN except ingress
- **C.** Routes it to DNS
- **D.** Floods all VLANs

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Floods eligible ports in the same VLAN except ingress**

If the receiver's MAC is unknown, the switch makes copies on eligible forwarding ports in that same VLAN, excluding the arrival port. It does not send those copies across every VLAN.

</details>

<a id="question-alignment-2"></a>

#### alignment-2

[Study objective 1.13](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-13)

Without NAT or tunneling, what normally changes as a router forwards an IPv4 packet onto another Ethernet link?

- **A.** Destination IP becomes the gateway IP
- **B.** Source and destination IPs swap
- **C.** Layer 2 addresses and TTL change; endpoint IPs remain
- **D.** The complete incoming frame remains unchanged

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. Layer 2 addresses and TTL change; endpoint IPs remain**

The router removes the incoming Ethernet wrapper, reduces IPv4 TTL by one and builds the next link's wrapper. The source and destination IP addresses normally remain the same unless another function, such as NAT or tunneling, changes them.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-13-same-port-filter"></a>

#### expanded-1.13-same-port-filter

[Study objective 1.13](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-13)

A switch receives a frame and finds its destination MAC learned on the same port where the frame arrived, in the same VLAN. What does it normally do?

- **A.** Always transmit it back to the ingress port.
- **B.** Filter the frame rather than send it back out that same port.
- **C.** Flood it out all VLANs including unrelated access VLANs.
- **D.** Route it using an OSPF neighbor table.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Filter the frame rather than send it back out that same port.**

The switch already knows the receiver is on the segment where the frame arrived. It therefore does not send the frame back out that same port or flood it elsewhere. This differs from having no known receiver entry.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-1-13-mac-move-and-aging"></a>

#### expanded-1.13-mac-move-and-aging

[Study objective 1.13](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-1-13)

A quiet endpoint is moved to a new switch port in the same VLAN. What most directly allows the switch to learn its new location?

- **A.** A received frame carrying that endpoint's source MAC on the new port.
- **B.** A DNS query that returns the old port number.
- **C.** The source MAC in a frame transmitted only by a different endpoint.
- **D.** Changing the endpoint's TCP destination port.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. A received frame carrying that endpoint's source MAC on the new port.**

The switch learns a device's location when it receives a frame with that device's source MAC on the new port. If the device remains silent, an old entry can remain until its aging timer removes it.

</details>

<a id="bank-domain-2"></a>

## 2.0 Network Access

### Objective 2.1 — Normal-range VLANs across switches

<a id="question-2-1-a"></a>

#### 2.1-a

[Study objective 2.1](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-1)

Two hosts in different VLANs need which function to communicate?

- **A.** Layer 3 routing
- **B.** A larger MAC table
- **C.** A hub
- **D.** A matching hostname

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Layer 3 routing**

VLANs create separate local Ethernet groups. A switch can deliver within one group, but moving an IP packet between their different subnets requires routing and usable gateways. Access rules can then limit that routed communication.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-1-access-membership-verification"></a>

#### expanded-2.1-access-membership-verification

[Study objective 2.1](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-1)

VLAN 30 exists on two switches and is allowed across their working trunk. One workstation cannot reach its same-VLAN peer. Which local check best tests whether its access port is in the correct VLAN?

- **A.** Create an OSPF area before checking the access port.
- **B.** Disable VLAN 30 on the remote switch.
- **C.** Change the peer to a different VLAN because same-VLAN communication requires routing.
- **D.** Inspect the port's operational access VLAN with show interfaces switchport.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Inspect the port's operational access VLAN with show interfaces switchport.**

Correct VLANs and a working trunk do not prove that the workstation's own socket belongs to VLAN 30. show interfaces switchport checks that port's operational access VLAN. Same-VLAN peers normally use switching rather than routing.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-1-selective-intervlan-policy"></a>

#### expanded-2.1-selective-intervlan-policy

[Study objective 2.1](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-1)

VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 must exchange routed traffic, while VLAN 30 must be isolated from both. All three have SVIs on a Layer 3 switch. Which design meets that requirement?

- **A.** Remove the VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 gateways while leaving VLAN 30 unrestricted.
- **B.** Use the same access VLAN on all ports and rely on separate subnet names.
- **C.** Keep the intended routing and apply an explicit filtering policy for VLAN 30, allowing the required VLAN 10-to-20 traffic.
- **D.** Assume different VLAN numbers automatically block traffic after routing is enabled.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. Keep the intended routing and apply an explicit filtering policy for VLAN 30, allowing the required VLAN 10-to-20 traffic.**

VLANs separate local delivery groups, but their working gateways can route between them. Apply deliberate rules to permit Users–Servers and block the required Guest directions, then test both allowed and blocked paths. Any required infrastructure exceptions must be explicit.

</details>

### Objective 2.2 — Links between switches

<a id="question-2-2-a"></a>

#### 2.2-a

[Study objective 2.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-2)

What happens to native-VLAN traffic on a default 802.1Q Cisco trunk?

- **A.** It is always dropped
- **B.** It is sent untagged
- **C.** It uses UDP encapsulation
- **D.** It is encrypted

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. It is sent untagged**

On a typical Cisco 802.1Q trunk, frames belonging to its native VLAN travel without a VLAN tag by default. Both ends must agree which VLAN that untagged traffic belongs to. Explicit native-tagging support can change this behavior.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-6"></a>

#### extra-6

[Study objective 2.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-2)

Why is a native VLAN mismatch a problem?

- **A.** Untagged frames can enter different VLANs at the two ends
- **B.** It disables every IP route
- **C.** It changes DNS records
- **D.** It makes all frames encrypted

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Untagged frames can enter different VLANs at the two ends**

Each trunk end puts untagged frames into its own configured native VLAN. If those settings differ, the same frame can be treated as belonging to different groups at the two ends.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-2-allowed-vlan-add"></a>

#### expanded-2.2-allowed-vlan-add

[Study objective 2.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-2)

An IOS XE trunk currently allows VLANs 10 and 20. VLAN 30 must be added while preserving those entries. Which interface command expresses that change?

- **A.** switchport trunk native vlan 30
- **B.** switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
- **C.** switchport trunk allowed vlan 30
- **D.** switchport access vlan 30

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30**

The add keyword extends the existing list while preserving 10 and 20. A list set to only 30 replaces the old list. Changing the native or access VLAN is a different action and does not add VLAN 30 to the allowed set.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-2-trunk-operational-check"></a>

#### expanded-2.2-trunk-operational-check

[Study objective 2.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-2)

A port's configuration includes switchport mode trunk, but VLAN 40 traffic does not cross it. Which verification directly checks both operational trunking and VLAN allowance?

- **A.** show interfaces trunk
- **B.** show ip nat translations
- **C.** show ntp associations
- **D.** show users

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. show interfaces trunk**

show interfaces trunk reports actual trunk operation and the relevant allowed, active and forwarding VLAN lists on supported switches. A configuration saying trunk expresses intent; it does not prove VLAN 40 is currently able to cross.

</details>

### Objective 2.3 — CDP and LLDP discovery

<a id="question-2-3-a"></a>

#### 2.3-a

[Study objective 2.3](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-3)

Which discovery protocol is vendor neutral?

- **A.** CDP
- **B.** LLDP
- **C.** DTP
- **D.** PAgP

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. LLDP**

LLDP is the multi-vendor discovery standard defined by IEEE 802.1AB. CDP is Cisco's own discovery protocol. Both describe directly connected neighbors rather than proving an entire application path works.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-3-neighbor-information-limit"></a>

#### expanded-2.3-neighbor-information-limit

[Study objective 2.3](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-3)

LLDP reports an adjacent switch and its connected port. What additional conclusion still requires separate verification?

- **A.** That the devices are physically or logically adjacent on that link.
- **B.** That the reported port identifier came from a discovery advertisement.
- **C.** That LLDP can exchange information between different vendors.
- **D.** Whether an end-to-end application path works across the network.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Whether an end-to-end application path works across the network.**

LLDP shows that local discovery messages from the adjacent device were received. It does not test the remote application, the return route, all required VLANs or permission rules along a complete path.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-3-interface-discovery-control"></a>

#### expanded-2.3-interface-discovery-control

[Study objective 2.3](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-3)

Security policy requires CDP disabled on one externally facing interface while retaining it on internal interfaces. Which IOS XE interface command has that scope?

- **A.** no ip routing
- **B.** lldp timer 30
- **C.** no cdp enable
- **D.** no cdp run

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. no cdp enable**

In interface mode, no cdp enable turns off CDP only on that selected connection. In global mode, no cdp run turns it off device-wide, which would also remove the intended internal discovery.

</details>

### Objective 2.4 — Layer 2 and Layer 3 LACP EtherChannels

<a id="question-2-4-a"></a>

#### 2.4-a

[Study objective 2.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-4)

Which LACP pairing forms a bundle?

- **A.** Passive / passive
- **B.** Active / passive
- **C.** On / passive
- **D.** Auto / auto

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Active / passive**

LACP active starts the bundle negotiation and passive responds. Active/passive can therefore form a bundle if the other link settings agree. Passive/passive leaves both sides waiting for someone else to start.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-7"></a>

#### extra-7

[Study objective 2.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-4)

A four-member EtherChannel carries one flow. What throughput should you expect?

- **A.** Always four times one link
- **B.** Generally limited by one member link
- **C.** Zero throughput
- **D.** Always equal to all members combined

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Generally limited by one member link**

A conversation is normally assigned to one member link so its packets remain ordered. Several conversations can use different members, increasing total bundle capacity without making one flow use all four links at once.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-4-routed-port-channel"></a>

#### expanded-2.4-routed-port-channel

[Study objective 2.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-4)

An IOS XE design uses an LACP EtherChannel as a routed link. Where is the link's Layer 3 address normally configured?

- **A.** On every member using the same connected IP address independently.
- **B.** On the logical routed Port-channel interface, with compatible routed member interfaces.
- **C.** On a different access VLAN on each physical member.
- **D.** Only on the neighbor's loopback, leaving the bundle without addressing.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. On the logical routed Port-channel interface, with compatible routed member interfaces.**

The routed bundle is one logical IP interface. Put its address on Port-channel and keep the physical members compatible and routed. Giving duplicate independent link addresses to members does not create the intended logical bundle.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-4-bundle-consistency"></a>

#### expanded-2.4-bundle-consistency

[Study objective 2.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-4)

LACP is active at both ends, but a proposed member is suspended after being assigned a different access VLAN from the existing bundle. What should be checked?

- **A.** Consistency of member and Port-channel switching parameters.
- **B.** Whether both peers can be changed to passive to force negotiation.
- **C.** Whether the bundle's DNS name is lowercase.
- **D.** Whether NTP uses TCP instead of UDP.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Consistency of member and Port-channel switching parameters.**

LACP active starts negotiation but does not make incompatible VLAN settings valid. Compare the intended member and Port-channel settings and correct the mismatch before expecting the member to join the bundle.

</details>

### Objective 2.5 — Rapid PVST+ operation

<a id="question-2-5-a"></a>

#### 2.5-a

[Study objective 2.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-5)

Which device becomes the STP root bridge?

- **A.** Highest MAC
- **B.** Lowest bridge ID
- **C.** Highest port number
- **D.** Lowest IP

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Lowest bridge ID**

Spanning Tree chooses the lowest bridge ID as its root reference. The configured priority is compared before the remaining identifying fields, so a lower priority value is preferred; the MAC address can break a later tie.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-8"></a>

#### extra-8

[Study objective 2.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-5)

What does BPDU guard do on an edge port receiving a BPDU?

- **A.** Normally err-disables the port
- **B.** Elects it root
- **C.** Enables a trunk
- **D.** Disables all VLANs

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Normally err-disables the port**

A BPDU is a spanning-tree control message. BPDU guard normally puts a protected endpoint port into an error-disabled state when one arrives, because an unexpected switch connection could threaten the intended edge design.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-9"></a>

#### extra-9

[Study objective 2.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-5)

Which RSTP state learns MACs but does not forward user frames?

- **A.** Learning
- **B.** Forwarding
- **C.** Disabled-root
- **D.** Listening

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Learning**

In Learning, RSTP can update the switch's MAC-to-port directory but still holds back ordinary user frames. Forwarding is the later state that permits user traffic; Discarding does not perform this learning step.

</details>

<a id="question-alignment-5"></a>

#### alignment-5

[Study objective 2.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-5)

Two candidate root ports have different total costs to the same root. What is compared first?

- **A.** Lower total root-path cost
- **B.** Highest sender bridge ID
- **C.** Lowest local IP
- **D.** VLAN name

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Lower total root-path cost**

First compare the total cost of each candidate path toward the root. The lower cost wins. Sender bridge and port identifiers are later tie-breakers, so they do not override an already lower path cost.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-5-root-guard-purpose"></a>

#### expanded-2.5-root-guard-purpose

[Study objective 2.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-5)

A downstream access switch must never become the STP root through its uplink. Which protection is designed to prevent a superior BPDU on the distribution port from changing the root placement?

- **A.** PortFast on every switch-to-switch link.
- **B.** A DNS forwarding cache.
- **C.** Disabling all BPDU transmission while leaving redundant links forwarding.
- **D.** Root guard.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Root guard.**

Root guard protects the chosen root location. A superior BPDU claims a better route/root than intended, so the protected port can be held root-inconsistent instead of accepting that claim. BPDU guard has a different endpoint-port purpose.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-5-loop-guard-purpose"></a>

#### expanded-2.5-loop-guard-purpose

[Study objective 2.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-5)

A redundant switch link stops receiving expected BPDUs even though the physical link remains up. Which STP protection helps prevent an inappropriate transition to forwarding caused by that loss?

- **A.** DHCP relay on the access VLAN.
- **B.** An increased DNS TTL for the switch.
- **C.** Loop guard on appropriate STP ports.
- **D.** PortFast on every redundant trunk.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. Loop guard on appropriate STP ports.**

Missing expected BPDUs can make a redundant path look safe when it is not. Loop guard can hold the affected port loop-inconsistent rather than let it incorrectly start forwarding. This differs from an edge port receiving an unexpected BPDU.

</details>

### Objective 2.6 — Wireless architectures and AP modes

<a id="question-2-6-a"></a>

#### 2.6-a

[Study objective 2.6](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-6)

Which AP mode supports local switching at a branch?

- **A.** Monitor
- **B.** Sniffer
- **C.** FlexConnect
- **D.** Spectrum-only

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. FlexConnect**

FlexConnect can put a branch client's traffic directly onto the branch's local wired VLAN. That avoids sending that locally switched data across the WAN to the controller, provided the intended branch settings and services exist.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-6-monitor-mode-ap"></a>

#### expanded-2.6-monitor-mode-ap

[Study objective 2.6](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-6)

An AP is assigned a dedicated monitoring role for RF observation rather than normal client service. What should users expect?

- **A.** It supplies PoE to its upstream switch.
- **B.** That AP is not intended to provide ordinary client access while in monitor mode.
- **C.** It necessarily becomes the default gateway for every client.
- **D.** It joins every client to an unencrypted SSID.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. That AP is not intended to provide ordinary client access while in monitor mode.**

A dedicated monitor-mode AP is assigned to observe the radio environment, not provide ordinary client access. Being powered and visible to management does not change that selected role.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-6-controller-and-autonomous"></a>

#### expanded-2.6-controller-and-autonomous

[Study objective 2.6](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-6)

A site has autonomous APs with individually maintained WLAN configuration. What operational change is central to adopting a controller-managed architecture?

- **A.** Move supported AP management and WLAN policy coordination into the controller-based workflow.
- **B.** Require every user packet to pass through the controller CPU in every supported mode.
- **C.** Eliminate the need for client authentication policy.
- **D.** Replace all radio channels with VLAN numbers.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Move supported AP management and WLAN policy coordination into the controller-based workflow.**

The controller-based workflow coordinates supported AP configuration and policy instead of maintaining each autonomous AP independently. Follow the architecture to determine the client data path; centralized management alone does not define it.

</details>

### Objective 2.7 — WLAN component connections

<a id="question-2-7-a"></a>

#### 2.7-a

[Study objective 2.7](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-7)

An SSID works at Layer 2 but clients get no address. Which service path should be checked?

- **A.** DHCP on the client VLAN
- **B.** STP bridge MAC only
- **C.** Console baud rate
- **D.** NTP stratum only

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. DHCP on the client VLAN**

The wireless connection can succeed while address assignment fails. Trace the client's VLAN to a working DHCP server or its configured relay, and check that the server has the correct address pool and a return path.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-7-ap-poe-and-uplink"></a>

#### expanded-2.7-ap-poe-and-uplink

[Study objective 2.7](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-7)

A newly installed lightweight AP has no LEDs and is absent from controller inventory. Which dependency should be verified first?

- **A.** The per-user RADIUS authorization result after association.
- **B.** The client's cached website password.
- **C.** The controller's preferred OSPF DR priority.
- **D.** Its supported power source and physical Ethernet uplink.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Its supported power source and physical Ethernet uplink.**

An unpowered AP cannot run its radios or join a controller. Check its compatible power source, remaining PoE power and cable first, before diagnosing wireless profiles or authentication policy.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-7-central-switching-path"></a>

#### expanded-2.7-central-switching-path

[Study objective 2.7](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-7)

In a centrally switched WLAN, the AP joins the controller successfully, but the controller's client-VLAN uplink path is broken. What outcome is plausible?

- **A.** Clients must automatically bypass the controller through local switching without configuration.
- **B.** All wired interfaces are necessarily physically down.
- **C.** AP management remains visible while client access to that wired VLAN fails.
- **D.** AP join proves every client VLAN is reachable end to end.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. AP management remains visible while client access to that wired VLAN fails.**

The AP's controller-management connection and the client's mapped data connection are separate paths. The AP can remain joined while a broken controller uplink VLAN prevents clients from reaching their gateway or services.

</details>

### Objective 2.8 — Network device management access

<a id="question-2-8-a"></a>

#### 2.8-a

[Study objective 2.8](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-8)

Which protocol encrypts a remote CLI session?

- **A.** Telnet
- **B.** SSH
- **C.** TFTP
- **D.** HTTP

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. SSH**

SSH encrypts the remote text-command session and supports identity checks. It protects the session in transit; a reachable management address, correct user authentication and suitable permissions are still separate requirements.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-8-https-management"></a>

#### expanded-2.8-https-management

[Study objective 2.8](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-8)

A device offers HTTP and HTTPS web management. Which choice protects credentials and page content in transit when properly configured with a validated certificate?

- **A.** Plain TFTP because it is connectionless.
- **B.** HTTPS.
- **C.** HTTP with a longer browser bookmark name.
- **D.** HTTP after disabling SSH.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. HTTPS.**

HTTPS uses TLS to protect the browser session in transit. Validate the device certificate and identity as well as supported settings; ordinary HTTP does not gain encryption from an unrelated configuration change.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-8-out-of-band-console"></a>

#### expanded-2.8-out-of-band-console

[Study objective 2.8](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-8)

A management-VLAN configuration error makes a switch unreachable by IP. A technician has authorized local access. Which path can restore CLI access without depending on that IP VLAN?

- **A.** The supported console connection.
- **B.** A new SSH session over the same broken management path.
- **C.** An HTTP request to an unrelated public DNS server.
- **D.** An SNMP poll sent to the wrong default gateway.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. The supported console connection.**

A supported console connection does not depend on the production management VLAN's IP reachability. It can provide authorized recovery access with the correct terminal settings and authentication even when that VLAN is misconfigured.

</details>

### Objective 2.9 — Wireless controller GUI settings

<a id="question-2-9-a"></a>

#### 2.9-a

[Study objective 2.9](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-9)

A WLAN is configured but its SSID is not advertised. Which setting should be checked first?

- **A.** WLAN enabled status
- **B.** NTP authentication
- **C.** OSPF cost
- **D.** PAT overload

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. WLAN enabled status**

A WLAN can exist in configuration while being turned off administratively. Check that it and the required related objects are enabled and assigned to the intended AP before expecting the network name to appear.

</details>

<a id="question-alignment-6"></a>

#### alignment-6

[Study objective 2.9](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-9)

Correct WLAN and policy profiles exist on a 9800, but the AP carries another policy tag. What should be inspected?

- **A.** Only the timezone
- **B.** The mapping in the policy tag actually applied to that AP
- **C.** Only the SSID spelling
- **D.** Conversion of DNS to TACACS+

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. The mapping in the policy tag actually applied to that AP**

On Catalyst 9800, the policy tag actually applied to the AP connects its WLAN with a policy profile. Correct profiles elsewhere do not prove that this AP is using the intended VLAN and rules.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-9-wlan-id-versus-ssid"></a>

#### expanded-2.9-wlan-id-versus-ssid

[Study objective 2.9](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-9)

An administrator is reviewing a controller GUI that shows both a WLAN profile name and an SSID. Which value identifies the wireless network name a client normally selects?

- **A.** The administrator's profile label in every controller implementation.
- **B.** The switch's EtherChannel number.
- **C.** The AP's console baud rate.
- **D.** The SSID.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. The SSID.**

The SSID is the network name the user normally sees and selects. A WLAN profile name or numeric identifier organizes the controller configuration and may be different from that visible name.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-2-9-gui-change-verification"></a>

#### expanded-2.9-gui-change-verification

[Study objective 2.9](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-2-9)

After changing a WLAN-to-VLAN mapping in a controller GUI, which evidence best validates the intended operational result?

- **A.** The administrator changes the dashboard color.
- **B.** The AP model name is visible in inventory.
- **C.** A test client receives settings from the intended subnet and reaches the permitted gateway/services.
- **D.** The browser displays a successful Save message, with no client test.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. A test client receives settings from the intended subnet and reaches the permitted gateway/services.**

A test client shows the policy actually in use: its VLAN/subnet, assigned settings and permitted connections. Saving a controller screen alone may miss a wrong profile assignment or a broken wired path.

</details>

<a id="bank-domain-3"></a>

## 3.0 IP Connectivity

### Objective 3.1 — Routing-table entries

<a id="question-3-1-a"></a>

#### 3.1-a

[Study objective 3.1](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-1)

In [110/20] on an OSPF route, what is 110?

- **A.** Hop count
- **B.** Administrative distance
- **C.** Prefix length
- **D.** Interface bandwidth

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Administrative distance**

IOS writes the two bracketed values as [administrative distance/metric]. In [110/20], 110 ranks this route source against other sources for the same prefix; 20 is OSPF's own path cost.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-1-connected-and-local-routes"></a>

#### expanded-3.1-connected-and-local-routes

[Study objective 3.1](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-1)

An IOS XE router has 192.0.2.1/24 configured on an up routed interface. Which routing-table entries normally identify the subnet and the router's own address?

- **A.** Two default routes with the interface MAC address as destination.
- **B.** A connected 192.0.2.0/24 entry and a local 192.0.2.1/32 entry.
- **C.** A local 192.0.2.0/24 entry and a connected default route.
- **D.** Only an OSPF external route to 192.0.2.1/24.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. A connected 192.0.2.0/24 entry and a local 192.0.2.1/32 entry.**

The connected /24 describes the attached subnet. The local /32 identifies packets addressed to the router's own 192.0.2.1 interface. The /32 entry does not change the subnet mask used by every host to /32.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-1-next-hop-versus-exit"></a>

#### expanded-3.1-next-hop-versus-exit

[Study objective 3.1](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-1)

A route lists next hop 198.51.100.2 and outgoing interface GigabitEthernet0/0. What do those fields represent?

- **A.** The adjacent forwarding target and the local interface used toward it.
- **B.** The final destination server and its physical switch port.
- **C.** The router's DNS server and an application socket.
- **D.** The route's administrative distance and metric.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. The adjacent forwarding target and the local interface used toward it.**

The next hop is the next forwarding target. GigabitEthernet0/0 is this router's own connection used toward it. Neither field is necessarily the final server, and neither is an administrative-distance or cost value.

</details>

### Objective 3.2 — Default forwarding decisions

<a id="question-3-2-a"></a>

#### 3.2-a

[Study objective 3.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-2)

A packet matches installed /16 and /24 routes. Which route is used?

- **A.** /16 with lower AD
- **B.** /24
- **C.** Whichever was learned first
- **D.** Neither

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. /24**

Both routes match, but /24 fixes more destination bits than /16 and covers a smaller address block. The router uses that more specific installed match. Administrative distance does not override it during this packet lookup.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-10"></a>

#### extra-10

[Study objective 3.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-2)

Two protocols offer the same /24. Which preference normally decides installation first?

- **A.** Lowest administrative distance
- **B.** Highest TCP port
- **C.** Lowest MAC
- **D.** Longest hostname

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. Lowest administrative distance**

For the identical destination prefix, administrative distance ranks different route sources. Lower is normally preferred. This is separate from choosing the longest matching prefix when forwarding a packet.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-2-no-match-no-default"></a>

#### expanded-3.2-no-match-no-default

[Study objective 3.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-2)

A router receives a packet whose destination matches no installed route, and no default route is present. What is its normal forwarding action?

- **A.** Flood the IP packet out every routed interface.
- **B.** Create a permanent host route from the packet's source MAC.
- **C.** Treat the DNS server as an automatic default gateway.
- **D.** Drop the packet rather than invent a route.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Drop the packet rather than invent a route.**

The router needs a matching installed route to choose a next step. With none, including no default, it drops the packet rather than guessing or flooding it like an unknown local Ethernet frame. Policy may permit an ICMP error response.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-2-same-protocol-metric"></a>

#### expanded-3.2-same-protocol-metric

[Study objective 3.2](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-2)

OSPF offers two otherwise eligible paths to the same prefix, with costs 20 and 35. Which path is preferred?

- **A.** Both solely because their prefix lengths are equal.
- **B.** The path received last, regardless of cost.
- **C.** The path with cost 20.
- **D.** The path with cost 35 because a higher metric is always preferred.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. The path with cost 20.**

For otherwise comparable OSPF paths to the same prefix, lower cost is better, so 20 beats 35. AD compares different route sources; longest-prefix matching later chooses between installed destination blocks for a packet.

</details>

### Objective 3.3 — IPv4 and IPv6 static routes

<a id="question-3-3-a"></a>

#### 3.3-a

[Study objective 3.3](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-3)

What makes a static route a floating backup?

- **A.** A lower prefix length
- **B.** An AD higher than the primary route
- **C.** A multicast next hop
- **D.** A loopback source

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. An AD higher than the primary route**

A floating route has a higher administrative distance than the preferred route for the same destination block. It stays less preferred while the primary is available and can become usable after the primary route disappears.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-13"></a>

#### extra-13

[Study objective 3.3](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-3)

Which IPv6 prefix represents a default route?

- **A.** ::/0
- **B.** ::1/128
- **C.** fe80::/10
- **D.** ff00::/8

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. ::/0**

::/0 fixes zero destination bits, so it matches every IPv6 destination. It is the default fallback and loses to any more specific installed route that also matches.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-3-ipv4-default-static-command"></a>

#### expanded-3.3-ipv4-default-static-command

[Study objective 3.3](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-3)

An IOS XE router must send destinations not matched by more-specific routes to reachable next hop 192.0.2.2. Which global command creates the required IPv4 static route?

- **A.** ipv6 route ::/128 192.0.2.2
- **B.** ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 192.0.2.2
- **C.** ip route 255.255.255.255 255.255.255.255 192.0.2.2
- **D.** ip default-gateway 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.0

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 192.0.2.2**

The all-zero destination and all-zero mask express 0.0.0.0/0, matching any IPv4 destination. It is used only when no more specific installed route matches. The next hop 192.0.2.2 and the return path still need to work.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-3-ipv6-link-local-next-hop"></a>

#### expanded-3.3-ipv6-link-local-next-hop

[Study objective 3.3](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-3)

An IOS XE IPv6 static route uses next-hop address fe80::2. Why must its exit interface also be specified?

- **A.** A link-local address is scoped to its link, so the router needs the interface to identify that link.
- **B.** Link-local addresses are globally unique Internet destinations.
- **C.** The interface converts the IPv6 prefix into an IPv4 mask.
- **D.** Every link-local address is a multicast group that must be flooded.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. A link-local address is scoped to its link, so the router needs the interface to identify that link.**

fe80::2 has only local-link scope, and the same written value could exist on more than one link. Naming the exit interface tells the router which link contains the intended neighbor.

</details>

### Objective 3.4 — Single-area OSPFv2

<a id="question-3-4-a"></a>

#### 3.4-a

[Study objective 3.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-4)

On a broadcast OSPF segment, which router is preferred as DR?

- **A.** Lowest router ID always
- **B.** Highest priority, then highest router ID
- **C.** Lowest interface IP always
- **D.** Newest neighbor

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Highest priority, then highest router ID**

At a broadcast-segment election, eligible routers compare interface priority first and router ID second, preferring higher values. Priority 0 is ineligible. A later better candidate does not automatically replace an already elected DR.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-11"></a>

#### extra-11

[Study objective 3.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-4)

Which OSPF interface priority makes a router ineligible for DR election?

- **A.** 0
- **B.** 1
- **C.** 100
- **D.** 255

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. 0**

An OSPF interface priority of 0 removes that interface from DR/BDR election eligibility. It can still participate in OSPF; it simply cannot win one of those coordinator roles on that segment.

</details>

<a id="question-extra-12"></a>

#### extra-12

[Study objective 3.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-4)

Does a new router with higher priority immediately replace an existing OSPF DR?

- **A.** Yes always
- **B.** No, election is nonpreemptive
- **C.** Only if it has IPv6
- **D.** Only on VLAN 1

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. No, election is nonpreemptive**

An established OSPF DR election is nonpreemptive. A new higher-priority router does not immediately take the current DR's role; priority influences an election when the protocol actually needs one.

</details>

<a id="question-alignment-8"></a>

#### alignment-8

[Study objective 3.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-4)

Two DROthers are 2-Way with each other and Full with the DR/BDR. What does that indicate?

- **A.** All priorities must become 255
- **B.** It can be normal broadcast-network behavior
- **C.** Their local process numbers must match
- **D.** Both database exchanges have failed

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. It can be normal broadcast-network behavior**

On a broadcast segment, ordinary routers called DROthers normally become Full with the DR/BDR coordinators, but can remain 2-Way with one another. Judge the state against the network type and roles before calling it a fault.

</details>

<a id="question-alignment-9"></a>

#### alignment-9

[Study objective 3.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-4)

What does network 10.1.12.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 primarily select in OSPF configuration?

- **A.** Remote router IDs starting 10.1.12
- **B.** TCP 89 sockets
- **C.** An arbitrary summary regardless of interfaces
- **D.** Local interfaces matching the address and wildcard

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Local interfaces matching the address and wildcard**

The address and wildcard select matching local router interfaces and assign them to area 0. The command does not simply instruct OSPF to advertise an arbitrary remote network that is not selected on a local interface.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-4-ospf-hello-area-mismatch"></a>

#### expanded-3.4-ospf-hello-area-mismatch

[Study objective 3.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-4)

Two directly connected OSPFv2 routers have unique router IDs and compatible addressing, but one interface is in area 0 and the other in area 1. What must be corrected for their normal neighbor relationship?

- **A.** Make their locally significant process IDs equal while keeping the area mismatch.
- **B.** Give both routers the same router ID.
- **C.** Disable the physical link to force a DR election.
- **D.** Put the connected OSPF interfaces in the same intended area.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Put the connected OSPF interfaces in the same intended area.**

OSPF neighbors on the shared connection must agree on their area. Correct the intended interfaces to the same area and check the other neighbor requirements. Their local process numbers may differ, while their router IDs should be unique.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-4-ospf-router-id-selection"></a>

#### expanded-3.4-ospf-router-id-selection

[Study objective 3.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-4)

An OSPFv2 process starts with no explicit router-id. It has loopback addresses 10.0.0.9 and 10.0.0.2 and an active physical address 203.0.113.254. Which router ID is normally selected?

- **A.** 10.0.0.2.
- **B.** 0.0.0.0 because private addresses cannot be router IDs.
- **C.** 10.0.0.9.
- **D.** 203.0.113.254.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**C. 10.0.0.9.**

With no configured router ID, eligible loopbacks are considered before physical interfaces. Of 10.0.0.9 and 10.0.0.2, .9 is higher, so it wins. Selection occurs when the process chooses its ID; a later address change need not replace an active ID.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-4-ospf-mtu-exchange"></a>

#### expanded-3.4-ospf-mtu-exchange

[Study objective 3.4](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-4)

Two OSPFv2 neighbors consistently stall in Exstart/Exchange. Area, timers and authentication match, but the interfaces use different IP MTUs. Which check best follows?

- **A.** Enable PortFast on the router process.
- **B.** Compare and reconcile the intended MTU settings and link support.
- **C.** Change the DNS suffix to match the OSPF process ID.
- **D.** Assume the adjacency is fully established because Hello packets are present.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. Compare and reconcile the intended MTU settings and link support.**

MTU is the maximum IP packet size supported on the link. Mismatched values can stop the routers exchanging their OSPF database descriptions even though initial neighbor messages work. Check and reconcile the intended actual link support.

</details>

### Objective 3.5 — First-hop redundancy concepts

<a id="question-3-5-a"></a>

#### 3.5-a

[Study objective 3.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-5)

What address should clients normally use with an FHRP?

- **A.** The standby physical address
- **B.** The virtual gateway IP
- **C.** The multicast group IP
- **D.** The router ID

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**B. The virtual gateway IP**

Clients use the shared virtual gateway IP. The physical router serving that identity can change after a detected failure, so clients do not need to replace their gateway setting with the other router's real address.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-5-fhrp-failover-arp"></a>

#### expanded-3.5-fhrp-failover-arp

[Study objective 3.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-5)

A working FHRP gateway fails over to its standby router. What allows hosts to continue using the same default-gateway configuration?

- **A.** The virtual gateway identity is taken over by the surviving router.
- **B.** Every host must be manually assigned the standby's physical interface address.
- **C.** The hosts automatically convert to Layer 2 switching between all subnets.
- **D.** DNS replaces the default route with an AP's BSSID.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**A. The virtual gateway identity is taken over by the surviving router.**

The surviving router takes over the shared virtual gateway identity. Hosts continue using the same virtual IP rather than being reconfigured to the survivor's physical address. The protocol's virtual-MAC and takeover mechanisms support local delivery.

</details>

<a id="question-expanded-3-5-fhrp-upstream-health"></a>

#### expanded-3.5-fhrp-upstream-health

[Study objective 3.5](LEARNING_PATH.md#objective-3-5)

An active gateway's LAN interface remains up, but its only upstream path fails. Why might a basic FHRP setup fail to restore off-subnet access by itself?

- **A.** FHRP always tests every application on every remote subnet.
- **B.** A virtual IP guarantees that all upstream routes are valid.
- **C.** A standby gateway must be in a different host subnet.
- **D.** Gateway-role availability alone does not necessarily track usable upstream reachability.

<details>
<summary>Answer and reasoning</summary>

**D. Gateway-role availability alone does not necessarily track usable upstream reachability.**
